text: The Supreme Court of Argentina, officially known as the Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation (Corte Suprema de Justicia de la Nación, CSJN), is the highest judicial body in the Argentine Nation and was inaugurated on 15 January 1863. Throughout much of the 20th century, the Court lacked independence from the executive branch, a situation that was formally addressed through reform enacted in 2003 by Decree 222/03. Functioning as a final appellate tribunal, its rulings are not subject to appeal and it holds the authority to interpret the constitution, including the power to invalidate laws deemed unconstitutional. Members are appointed by the President with the agreement of at least two-thirds of the Senate, convened specifically for this purpose, and can only be removed through an impeachment process called juicio político, initiated by the Chamber of Deputies and conducted by the Senate on grounds of improper conduct. The Court is headquartered in the Palacio de Justicia in the San Nicolás neighborhood of Buenos Aires, a building designed by French architect Norbert Maillart in 1906 and inaugurated in 1910, with further developments completed by 1942. Notable artistic installations include Justice by Rogelio Yrurtia and José de San Martín by Luis Perlotti. At the start of the 20th century, the Court consisted of five magistrates. After the 1930 military coup led by José Félix Uriburu, which began the Infamous Decade, the five justices acknowledged the new regime and formally ended constitutional order, setting a precedent that influenced Argentina’s political trajectory. During Juan Perón’s presidency, the Court approved decrees not passed by Congress. In 1947, following a conservative military phase, Perón initiated a trial against three judges, resulting in one resignation and only one judge remaining in office. From 1946 to 1955, the judiciary aligned with Justicialist policies. After the 1955 Revolución Libertadora, the five justices were removed by the military. When Arturo Frondizi’s constitutional government took office in 1958, three judges resigned; during his term, the number of judges increased and all Peronist judges were removed. In 1963, Arturo Illia’s democratic government sought to expand the Court’s size, but the military coup led by Juan Carlos Onganía (Revolución Argentina) deposed Illia before implementation. Upon taking power, the military pressured the judges to resign, a move reversed only shortly before the return of constitutional order in 1973. On 24 May 1973, an ad hoc tribunal was established with five Peronist judges, none of whom had prior judicial experience. After the March 1976 military coup, the junta attempted to remove all justices, who accepted an act outlining the objectives of the "National Reorganization Process," which led to widespread state repression and the disappearance of 30,000 people. Under Carlos Menem’s presidency, the executive exerted significant pressure on the judiciary. In 1989, Menem expanded the Court from five to nine members and selected four new justices; the Senate approved the appointments on 19 April 1990 during a secret session lasting seven minutes, without opposition. The resignation of judge Bacqué ensured Menem’s party held an absolute majority. In 1994, a constitutional reform modified the nomination process: while the executive still proposes candidates and the Senate approves them, an absolute majority was no longer required—only two-thirds of the current Senate members were needed. The reform also introduced amparo, hábeas corpus, and hábeas data. In the 2000s, especially during Néstor Kirchner’s presidency beginning in 2003, all members of Menem’s majority either resigned or were removed; Dr. Antonio Boggiano, the last, was removed on 29 September 2005, leaving two vacancies. The amicus curiae process, allowing third parties to submit written arguments on behalf of public interest, was formalized; it was used in 2001 when Spanish authorities issued an international arrest warrant for human rights violators in Argentina, and an NGO submitted a text advocating for either extradition or prosecution under subsidiary universal jurisdiction. This contributed to the 2005 ruling in the Caso Simon case, which declared forced disappearances as crimes against humanity. Two years earlier, Congress had declared the 1986 Ley de Punto Final and 1987 Ley de Obediencia Debida amnesty laws unconstitutional, enabling trials of human rights violators from the dictatorship. In 2003, a key reform was implemented: starting 19 June 2003, presidential decrees required the executive to nominate candidates for Supreme Court seats, with public disclosure of nominees’ resumes by the Ministry of Justice, allowing public, NGO, academic, and professional scrutiny. After three months, the President could present the nominee to the Senate, which required a two-thirds majority for approval. On 2 July 2003, the Senate approved a reform requiring its commission to publicly disclose its decisions on judicial and public ministry nominations. Following a colloquium by the CELS NGO, Chief Justice Petracchi agreed to publish the Court’s decisions. In late 2006, several justices criticized President Menem’s delay in appointing the two vacancies, noting that a nine-member Court requires a five-member majority for consensual decisions, and demanded either appointments for Augusto Belluscio and Antonio Boggiano or a congressional law reducing the Court to seven justices. In May 2025, while compiling historical documents for a national museum, the Court discovered materials linked to the Nazi regime intended to spread fascist ideology in Argentina and across South America. On 20 June 1941, 83 packages from the German Embassy in Tokyo, transported via the Japanese Steamship Nan-a-Maru, arrived in Buenos Aires. The German diplomatic mission requested their release, claiming they contained "personal belongings," but the Customs and Ports Division retained them indefinitely. Upon discovery, Supreme Court President Horacio Rosatti ordered their preservation for historical analysis. The Court has historically played a significant role in shaping national policy, engaging with political, social, and institutional issues, often going beyond mere legal interpretation. Notable examples include early protections of property rights during inflation and support for divorce before legislative enactment. In the landmark 1961 Manzanares case, the Court affirmed that judges contribute to the creation of justice alongside lawmakers. Legal philosopher Carlos Santiago Nino emphasized the judiciary’s role in protecting democratic procedures and ensuring fair justice distribution. During the 1980s, the Court was instrumental in restoring democracy and institutional stability after Argentina’s return to civilian rule. The Court’s geographic coordinates are 34°36′08″S 58°23′10″W (34.60222°S 58.38611°W).
